'''Laver's theorem''', in [[order theory]], states that [[order embedding|order embeddability]] of countable [[total order]]s is a [[well-quasi-ordering]]. That is, for every infinite [[sequence]] of totally-ordered [[countable set]]s, there exists an order embedding from an earlier member of the sequence to a later member. This result was previously known as '''Fraïssé's conjecture''', after [[Roland Fraïssé]], who conjectured it in 1948;{{r|fraisse}} [[Richard Laver]] proved the conjecture in 1971. More generally, Laver proved the same result for order embeddings of countable unions of [[scattered order]]s.{{r|harzheim|laver}}

In [[reverse mathematics]], the version of the theorem for countable orders is denoted FRA (for Fraïssé) and the version for countable unions of scattered orders is denoted LAV (for Laver).{{r|hirschfeldt}} In terms of the "big five" systems of [[second-order arithmetic]], FRA is known to fall in strength somewhere between the strongest two systems, <math>\Pi_1^1</math>-CA<sub>0</sub> and ATR<sub>0</sub>, and to be weaker than <math>\Pi_1^1</math>-CA<sub>0</sub>.  However, it remains open whether it is equivalent to ATR<sub>0</sub> or strictly between these two systems in strength.{{r|montalban}}
